---
title: "Remote Devboxes"
description: "Run heavy Tuturuuu development workflows on self-hosted remote runners."
---

## Overview

Remote devboxes let internal root workspace members offload expensive local work
to self-hosted runner machines. A runner connects outbound to `tuturuuu.com`,
receives queued work, executes it on its host, streams logs, stores artifacts,
and releases the lease automatically for one-off work.

The current `ttr box agent` executes claimed commands as child processes on its
host. Its command policy and environment filtering are operational controls,
not an isolation boundary for untrusted learner code. Do not route Learn coding
submissions to ordinary Devbox runs. Judge needs a separate sandbox executor
and readiness checks before its capability can be enabled.

V1 is intentionally self-hosted. It does not provision cloud machines. Any
runner host should have Node.js, Bun, Docker, and Git available.

## Quick Start

```bash
ttr login
ttr box doctor
ttr box setup
ttr box setup --dir .
ttr box setup --dir . --clone-into ./tuturuuu
ttr box agent register --name "ci-lab-1"
ttr box agent start --token <runner-token>
ttr box repair --dir .
ttr box upgrade --runner <runner-id>
ttr box restart --runner <runner-id>
TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_RUNNER_TOKEN=<runner-token> ttr box shutdown
```

`ttr box setup` is the default bootstrap for a runner host. It first checks
whether the current directory is already a Tuturuuu platform checkout. If it is,
setup reuses that checkout. Otherwise it can clone or reuse
`https://github.com/tutur3u/platform.git`, install dependencies with
`bun install --frozen-lockfile`, start local Supabase with `bun sb:start`,
verify `supabase status -o json`, and write local Supabase connection values
into ignored `apps/*/.env.local` files. Secret values are redacted from human
and JSON output.

Pass `--dir <path>` for a specific checkout. If the target exists but is not a
valid Tuturuuu checkout, interactive setup asks whether it should clone into a
nested `tuturuuu` directory. In non-interactive shells, pass
`--clone-into <path>` explicitly:

```bash
ttr box setup --dir . --clone-into ./tuturuuu
```

Use `--yes` only when the host should install detected missing prerequisites
automatically. Runner registration and service installation are separate
choices.

To register the machine and install a boot-starting runner service in one
non-interactive command after login:

```bash
ttr box setup --agent --service --runner-name "$(hostname)-devbox" --yes
```

For a platform runner that does not need a Tuturuuu checkout or local Supabase,
use `ttr box connect --service --runner-name "$(hostname)-devbox"` instead.
This registers the machine, writes its runner token to a mode-0600 file, and
installs the same boot-starting service. The CLI prints a direct Infrastructure
dashboard link for that runner. The dashboard shows the heartbeat's CLI version
and machine identity so an administrator can verify the connection before
enabling workloads.

The setup command stores the runner token in a restricted local env file and
installs a system-level runner service on Linux systemd or macOS launchd. The
service starts after reboot and restarts automatically if the runner exits.
Runner heartbeats report a small observability snapshot, including `ttr`, Bun,
Node, Docker, Git, OS, CPU, RAM, load average, and uptime. Root workspace admins
can inspect those fields from Infrastructure > Devboxes.

Devbox agent poll and heartbeat traffic is blocked by default at the platform
API boundary. Set `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_AGENT_API_ENABLED=true` on the web app before
starting or repairing runners. When the flag is absent, agent poll and heartbeat
requests return `403` before runner tokens are authenticated or runner state is
updated.

### Cloudflare control plane

`ttr box agent start` uses the existing web API until
`TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_CONTROL_URL` is set on the runner host. Point this variable
at the deployed `tuturuuu-devbox-control` Worker to send heartbeats, job claims,
and an authenticated wake connection through Cloudflare. The agent still sends
job events and completion to the web API. It polls the Worker every 30 seconds
when idle, even with a wake connection, so a missed signal cannot strand work.
The Worker checks the runner token, token revocation, runner status, and root
workspace membership before each heartbeat or claim. Disabling heartbeats on
a runner continues to reject heartbeat requests. Worker traffic requires TLS.
Agents treat `401` as fatal, so `401` means only that the credentials were
rejected. If token, runner or membership storage fails, the web agent routes
return `503` with `Retry-After: 5`, and the Worker returns `503`. Agents then
back off and retry instead of exiting and flapping during a database brownout
(`agent-auth.test.ts`).

The production workflow installs Worker secrets from the repository's
`PRODUCTION_SUPABASE_URL`, `PRODUCTION_SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`, and
`DEVBOX_CONTROL_INTERNAL_TOKEN` secrets. It uses
`COLAB_CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` for Cloudflare deployment. Set
`TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_CONTROL_URL` and `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_CONTROL_TOKEN` on web and
Learn to wake an assigned runner immediately after enqueuing work. Use the
same internal token as the Worker secret; never put it in the runner's env file.
Missing or failed wake calls do not fail enqueue, and the fallback poll catches
the job. Verify `/health`, then a real runner heartbeat, claim, completion,
revocation rejection, and Learn submission before moving additional runners.
The old web API remains available until all runners are migrated.

Without a Worker URL, idle claims back off from 5 to 10, 20, and then 30 seconds.
A claimed job or completion resets that delay; heartbeats remain independent at
20 seconds to preserve online detection and leases. Worker wake messages still
trigger immediate claims, with a 30-second reconciliation poll for missed wakes.

If a host completed `ttr box setup` but does not appear in Infrastructure >
Devboxes, confirm it was registered as a runner. Plain setup prepares the
checkout, dependencies, local Supabase, and ignored env files only; it does not
create a `private.devbox_runners` row. Run setup with `--agent --service`, or
register and start the agent manually, then confirm `ttr whoami` on that host is
pointing at the same production origin and root workspace user.

If the host appears as registered but shows no heartbeat, inspect the installed
service on that host:

```bash
sudo systemctl status --no-pager --full tuturuuu-devbox-runner.service
sudo journalctl -u tuturuuu-devbox-runner.service -n 80 --no-pager
```

The runner service reads its token from the local `devbox-runner.env` file. If
the journal shows a missing runner token or stale wrapper, upgrade the CLI and
repair the service. Repair reuses the existing token file; it does not register
a new runner token or create another runner row.

```bash
ttr upgrade
ttr box repair --dir .
```

Use dry-run first when you want to confirm the checkout, token file, service
manager, wrapper path, and service path without writing files or calling sudo:

```bash
ttr box repair --dir . --dry-run
```

Upgrade a runner's global CLI through the same brokered queue:

```bash
ttr box upgrade --runner <runner-id>
```

The upgrade command queues `bun i -g tuturuuu` for the selected runner, waits
for completion, and returns the remote command logs and exit code. After a
successful CLI update, the agent exits; a runner installed with `--service`
restarts under systemd or launchd and reports its new CLI version on the next
heartbeat. A manually started agent must be restarted by its operator. The run
completion and the subsequent heartbeat are separate verification steps.

### Platform-owned fleet controls

Root members can use the existing Infrastructure authorization boundary through
`client.devboxes.fleet.snapshot()` or the CLI:

```bash
ttr box runners --json
ttr box inspect --runner <id> --json
ttr box upgrade --runners <id,id> --dry-run
ttr box upgrade --runners <id,id> --apply --json
ttr box restart --all --dry-run
```

Fleet maintenance defaults to a dry run. `--apply` performs sequential,
allowlisted maintenance, rechecks fresh heartbeats and unfinished work before
each operation, stops on failure, and waits for a subsequent healthy heartbeat.
Upgrades additionally verify the advertised CLI version against the registry
release. Offline, revoked, busy, or truncated snapshots are skipped. Snapshot
limits mean this is a conservative operator convenience, not an atomic host-wide
reservation; coordinate a maintenance window when service users share an install.
Capabilities, feature switches, and resource limits are available as structured
JSON for tooling extensions. These commands do not enable arbitrary shell access
or change runner workload permissions. Custom SDK deployments use their own
origin rather than forwarding credentials to hosted Infrastructure.

### Runner trust pools and drain

Trusted workloads (`run`, `build`, `serve`, `tunnel`) and untrusted Judge or
playground work never share a runner identity. Give each trust tier its own
runner token, OS user, token file, service unit and Docker socket.
`set_devbox_runner_feature` refuses to enable trusted features on a runner with
Judge or playground enabled, or one that reports `executionMode: judge-only`, and
the reverse for Judge and playground. A reported mode can only narrow what may be
enabled; it never grants a feature. The function locks the runner row before
checking, so concurrent toggles or a concurrent heartbeat cannot leave a runner
with both tiers enabled. Newly registered runners start with every feature off,
so an operator must enable features explicitly. This includes runners a non-root
user registers with `ttr box register` or `ttr box connect`: they accept no work,
not even trusted `run` jobs from their owner, until a root Infrastructure admin
enables a feature through the dashboard or the features endpoint below. Existing
runners keep their features, including legacy runners that already mix tiers.

Draining a runner stops all new claims on it except maintenance (restart or
upgrade). New Judge and playground enqueues skip draining runners, and creating a
non-maintenance run pinned to one (`--runner`, or a lease on it) fails with
`Runner is draining`; a database trigger enforces this for every insert path.
Queued Judge work pinned to it is requeued to another Judge runner that enqueue
would also choose: it must support the submission's language, report no
`trusted` mode, and have no trusted feature enabled. Its lease moves with it.
Queued Judge work whose lease has expired, and other queued work pinned to it
(explicit `--runner` pins, playground environments), is cancelled with a run
event, and its idle non-kept leases are released. In-flight jobs finish
normally. Requesting a drain again re-runs these sweeps. Judge work that no
other runner can take stays queued until its lease expires.

The Infrastructure snapshot (`ttr box runners --json`) reports per-runner
`drain_requested_at`, uncapped `activity` counts and `drained`. `active_leases`
counts unexpired non-kept leases; `kept_leases` counts persistent leases, which a
drain never releases and which do not block `drained`. Release kept leases
separately before retiring the runner. `drained` is true once a draining runner
has no queued or running work and no active leases.
These fields are `null` until the migration is applied. Operators with the
dashboard's root secrets or roles permission can call:

```bash
POST /api/v1/infrastructure/devboxes/runners/<runner-id>/features  {"feature":"judge","enabled":false}
POST /api/v1/infrastructure/devboxes/runners/<runner-id>/drain     {"draining":true}
```

Both use the same guarded database functions as the dashboard. Regression
coverage lives in `apps/database/supabase/tests/devbox-runner-trust-pools.sql`
and `devbox-runner-drain-hardening.sql` (pgTAP), and the Infrastructure route
and store tests.

### Claim admission by reported execution mode

The database flag `private.devbox_control_settings.require_reported_execution_mode`
defaults to off and must stay off pending agent and heartbeat-handler support.
Judge always refuses a runner reporting `trusted`, even when this flag is off.
With the flag on, `claim_next_devbox_run` additionally enforces trusted-work
report freshness:

- `run`, `build`, `serve` and `tunnel` claims require the runner to have
  reported `executionMode: trusted` within the last 90 seconds;
- Judge claims refuse every runner reporting `trusted`, even with a stale or
  missing timestamp. `judge-only` and legacy agents without a mode remain eligible;
- playground and maintenance claims are unchanged.

Report freshness uses `capabilities_updated_at`, which a database trigger owns and stamps
on inserts and every capabilities or timestamp update. A trusted report older than the
window cannot admit trusted work; future timestamps are rejected. Identical
reports and timestamp-only writes are restamped by the server. The agent's clock
is never trusted.

Agents report `executionMode` from `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_EXECUTION_MODE`, and both the
web heartbeat schema and the control Worker's capability allowlist accept it as a
string enum. Before cutover, deploy agents that report it and verify a fresh
trusted report from every run-enabled runner; keep the admission flag off until
that verification.

An authorized operator runs
`private.set_devbox_require_reported_execution_mode(true)` through the gated
production database path. It refuses while any run-enabled runner lacks a fresh
`trusted` report and lists those runners; `p_force => true` overrides that guard
deliberately; NULL does not override it, and NULL `p_enabled` is rejected. Disable the flag the same way with `false`. Regression coverage
lives in `apps/database/supabase/tests/devbox-claim-mode-admission.sql`.
### Several runner identities on one host

Keep each trust tier on its own runner identity: a separate runner token, OS
user, token file, service unit and Docker socket. Pass `--service-name <name>`
to `ttr box setup`, `ttr box connect` and `ttr box repair` to give an identity
its own systemd unit (`tuturuuu-devbox-runner-<name>.service`), launchd label
(`com.tuturuuu.devbox-runner.<name>`), token file (`devbox-runner-<name>.env`)
and wrapper. Without a name the legacy single-runner paths are used, so existing
installations and `repair` keep working. `setup`, `connect` and `repair` refuse
to overwrite a token file, wrapper or unit that belongs to a different execution
mode (for example adding a Judge runner without a name on a host whose legacy
unit is trusted). Use `--service-name` for the new identity; pass `--force` only
to deliberately replace the existing one. `repair --execution-mode` still
requires `--force` when the installed service belongs to another mode.

The agent enforces the tiers locally as well. A `trusted` runner never executes
Judge or playground envelopes. A playground pool process
(`TUTURUUU_PLAYGROUND_POOL_ID`) accepts only playground envelopes and
maintenance. A `judge-only` runner accepts only Judge envelopes and maintenance.
Judge hosts therefore run in `judge-only` mode, which `--judge-images` selects
automatically. When a trusted runner refuses a Judge or playground envelope it
posts `trusted_runner_fence refused a <judge|playground> envelope` as the job
error and logs `[devbox] trusted_runner_fence` locally. That means untrusted work
was routed to a credentialed host: audit run events for it before enabling
trusted-mode admission.

`ttr box doctor --isolation` prints read-only evidence about the identity it
runs as: dedicated user, private token directory, systemd `ProtectHome`,
dedicated Docker socket, gVisor default runtime, and no `docker` group
membership. Each check is `pass`, `FAIL` or `unknown`. The command exits `1`
unless every check the execution mode requires is proven and no other
non-advisory check fails. `trusted` requires a dedicated user and a private
token directory; `judge-only` also requires a dedicated Docker socket, gVisor
by default and no `docker` group. An unset `DOCKER_HOST` with a reachable
daemon counts as the general socket. `protectedService` is advisory: it is
self-reported and an unreadable `/home` is reported as `unknown`, never a pass.
The mode comes from `--execution-mode` or `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_EXECUTION_MODE`.
Add `--other-user <judge-user>` to prove that user cannot reach this runner's
secrets. It fails when that user is root or in `docker`, `sudo`, `wheel`,
`admin`, `root` or `lxd`; when the credential file or directory is a symlink,
or grants it owner, group or other access. It checks `$HOME`, the checkout
(`--checkout-dir`, default cwd), checkout `.env*` files other than examples,
and every ancestor using modes and ACLs (`getfacl` on Linux, `ls -le` on macOS).
Effective extended ACL grants conservatively fail even for unrelated identities;
missing tools or indeterminate ACLs are required `unknown` failures. Agents
report `executionMode` and the isolation summary in heartbeats only when
`TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_REPORT_EXECUTION_MODE=true` is set. Enable it only after both
heartbeat handlers accept those fields.

### Running an exact commit

Trusted runners accept a typed `__ttr_commit_run_v1__` envelope that carries
only a full commit SHA, a clean relative directory, and an argv. The runner
checks the argv against the execution policy before any git work, then fetches
`origin` branches (`refs/heads/*` into `refs/remotes/origin/*`) and requires
the SHA to be reachable from one of them. A commit that GitHub would serve by
SHA from elsewhere in a fork network is rejected. The detached worktree is
created inside a fresh `mkdtemp` directory (mode `0700`) under the runner-private
`commit-runs` directory beside the CLI config, never in shared `/tmp`. The argv
then runs from that directory through the normal execution policy,
process-group timeout and stop handling, and the worktree is removed on every
exit path. Agent startup removes any `ttr-commit-run-*` worktree a crashed agent
left behind and prunes git's records. Local edits on the requesting machine and
on the runner never reach the run. Unknown commits and missing directories fail
before anything runs. Git error output is not forwarded, because remote URLs can contain
credentials. `judge-only` runners and playground pools reject the envelope.
`ttr resources run --offload` uses it.

A runner advertises the envelope versions it decodes as
`capabilities.protocols.commitRun` (currently `[1]`). The advertisement ships in
the same build as the decoder and is sent only by opted-in (`TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_REPORT_EXECUTION_MODE=true`)
`trusted` runners. `ttr resources run --offload` submits a commit run only to a
runner that advertises the client's version. Otherwise the runner is
`blockedBy=capability_missing`: `auto` queues locally and an explicit runner ID
fails. This closes the gap where an older trusted runner would execute the
envelope as a command. Deploy the heartbeat handlers that accept `protocols`
before upgrading trusted runners, because both handlers reject unknown keys.

The server enforces the same rule, so direct submissions and capability changes
after selection cannot bypass it (migration
`20261024030400_devbox_commit_run_protocol.sql`):

- Both heartbeat handlers drop `protocols` unless the report says
  `executionMode: trusted`. A database trigger also drops it for any runner with
  Judge or playground enabled.
- A run whose command is the envelope must be pinned, through `runnerId` and an
  automatic lease, to a runner that supports the protocol now. The create handler
  returns 400 or 409, and the `require_devbox_commit_run_runner` trigger enforces
  the same rule against races.
- If a claim would hand the envelope to an unsupported runner (for example after
  re-pinning), the `refuse_unsupported_devbox_commit_run_claim` trigger skips it.
  It also expires the run's lease so the run is no longer offered, and records a
  refusal event. Stop the run and submit it again.
- When a runner stops advertising support, the
  `cancel_unsupported_devbox_commit_runs` trigger cancels its queued envelope runs.

`claim_next_devbox_run` is not redefined, so concurrent changes to its body stay
intact. `apps/database/supabase/tests/devbox-commit-run-protocol.sql` covers these
rules against the real claim function.

### Protecting hosts with existing critical files

Use `--execution-mode judge-only` with `box connect`, `box setup`, or `box
repair`. Supplying Judge images during registration defaults to Judge-only;
general development runners retain trusted execution. Manual Judge-only setup
restricts accepted jobs but does not receive protected-service host isolation;
use the protected Linux service setup for hosts with critical files. `--control-url` persists
the HTTPS Cloudflare Worker URL during registration. Protected service setup
requires Linux systemd, a pre-existing non-login service user with its private
home under `/var/lib`, a private service-owned token directory, and checkout and
CLI outside personal homes. The dedicated root-owned Unix Docker socket must be
mode `0660` and restricted to that user's group; the user must not belong to the general
`docker` group. Preflight verifies the daemon defaults to `runsc` with cgroup
limits before registering a credential. It does not create OS users, move host
files, or reconfigure a shared Docker daemon automatically.

```bash
ttr box connect --service --service-manager systemd --service-user tuturuuu-judge \
  --execution-mode judge-only --docker-host unix:///run/tuturuuu-judge-docker/docker.sock \
  --token-file /var/lib/tuturuuu-judge/config/runner.env --judge-images "$TUTURUUU_JUDGE_IMAGES"
```

Run protected setup and repair as root from the prepared runner directory, using
an authenticated operator CLI context and a CLI installed outside personal homes.
The installer deliberately fails before registration when invoked by a non-root
operator: it does not broaden private directory permissions or implicitly copy
operator credentials into the service account. Prepare the token directory with
mode `0700`; group and other access are rejected. Protected systemd units hide personal homes, make the host
filesystem read-only except runner directories, remove capabilities, restrict
devices, namespaces and kernel access, and set a private umask. Repair preserves
an existing Judge-only policy and refuses to weaken it; `--dry-run` performs the
same preflight before service writes. Setup persists the dedicated service user
for subsequent repair. Older private token files need `--service-user` once;
repair then retains it without rotating the runner token. The wrapper prefers the service user's
global `ttr` executable so upgrades affect the running service. Before starting
a protected agent, it requires `box agent policy` to succeed on that executable;
an older CLI lacking policy support fails closed rather than launching. Launchd lacks
these Linux protections; use a dedicated Linux VM for protected Judge setup on
macOS. Local policy enforcement requires the CLI release containing this change.

Judge-only servers must keep Run, Build, Preview, and Tunnel disabled in
Infrastructure. Set `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_EXECUTION_MODE=judge-only` in the private
runner environment after installing the release containing this local policy.
It rejects host commands, environment files, and environment overrides on
maintenance jobs even if a remote workload switch is accidentally enabled.
Unknown modes fail closed. The exact CLI-update and supervised-restart commands
remain root-member-authorized maintenance operations.

Judge submissions use digest-pinned images, gVisor `runsc`, an unprivileged
container user, no network, a read-only root filesystem, no host bind mounts,
dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation, and CPU/memory/PID/time limits.
Never expose the Docker socket to submissions. The runner and dedicated Docker
daemon remain trusted infrastructure: access to a rootful Docker socket is a
privileged control plane, even when its default runtime is gVisor. Keep the
service user out of the general Docker group, use a dedicated Unix socket, hide
personal home directories, and do not use this host for arbitrary trusted devbox
commands. Stronger isolation for additional workloads requires a separate VM or
host; a shell-command denylist is not a security boundary.

### Operator-owned automatic upgrades

For a fleet whose service users do not have CLI user sessions, schedule upgrades
from an authenticated operator machine with an explicit runner allowlist:

```bash
bun scripts/devbox-cli-upgrades.ts --runner <id> --runner <id>
bun scripts/devbox-cli-upgrades.ts --runner <id> --runner <id> --apply
bun scripts/setup-devbox-cli-upgrades.ts --runner <id> --runner <id> --dry-run
bun scripts/setup-devbox-cli-upgrades.ts --runner <id> --runner <id>
```

The installer supports macOS launchd, checks at login and every 24 hours while
the operator machine is running, and stores its portable script, lock helper, and private
logs under `~/.tuturuuu/devbox-upgrades`. It uses the existing CLI session and
never copies credentials into its plist. `launchctl print
gui/$(id -u)/com.tuturuuu.devbox-cli-upgrades` shows scheduler status. A full
snapshot, an active lease, stale heartbeat, or unfinished job prevents upgrade;
an unsuccessful run or version heartbeat stops the remaining operations.
Keep runner self-upgrades disabled when this scheduler owns maintenance.

Ensure the service's executable points at the same global installation that
`bun i -g tuturuuu` updates for its OS user. A successful install into a different
path does not update a service launching an older private copy. After changing a
systemd path, drain work, reload the unit, restart sequentially, and verify each
runner's heartbeat and CLI version.

### Automatic CLI upgrades

New or repaired managed services default `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_AUTO_UPGRADE=false`.
Enable `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_AUTO_UPGRADE=true` in the private runner environment only
after selecting an upgrade owner and maintenance policy. Existing services need one repair after the
release containing this capability is installed:

```bash
ttr box repair --dir . --dry-run
ttr box repair --dir .
```

An idle agent checks the official npm registry at most once per day, installs
only a newer stable `tuturuuu` release pinned to its exact version, verifies
`--version`, and exits for its service manager to restart. It pauses new claims
during installation and keeps heartbeating. A private host lock serializes
installs from runners sharing an OS user home directory, and persisted check state
prevents restart retry loops. Cached install state is scoped to the verified
CLI command, and a failed cached-version verification resumes its registry check. Other agents using that shared install restart
after verifying the installed version. Lock contention schedules another attempt
after 30 seconds, at the next idle claim, rather than delaying a stale process
for a full day. Registry checks remain limited by the shared daily state. Each agent drains its own jobs; for hosts
with different OS service users or unrelated CLI consumers, coordinate a
host maintenance window or opt out instead of assuming this lock covers them.

Installer subprocesses receive host path/runtime variables, never the runner
token. An unverified install attempts to restore the previous release. A failed
rollback stops the agent with a repair error; inspect service logs and repair
the host installation. Locks record process ownership and identity; dead owners are reclaimed under a
separate reclamation guard, while live installers are never evicted by age. An
unknown legacy lock requires operator inspection. Reclaim guards also record
process ownership; an interrupted guard reports a repair-required error rather
than being deleted automatically or retrying silently. Never remove a lock held by a running installer.

Set `TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_AUTO_UPGRADE=false` in `devbox-runner.env` to opt out.
Manually started and source-checkout agents do not upgrade automatically unless
explicitly configured, and source `.ts` entry points never mutate the global CLI.
Infrastructure's **Update CLI** remains the bootstrap for existing runners;
confirm both its successful run and the subsequent version heartbeat. Source
changes take effect only after the normal tested CLI release is published.

Regression coverage: `devbox-auto-upgrade.test.ts` covers stable version
validation, pinned installation, shared-host locking, restart throttling,
verification and rollback. `devbox-agent.test.ts` covers claim backoff,
independent heartbeats, concurrency, draining and supervised restart;
`devbox-setup.test.ts` verifies the service wrapper preserves the explicit opt-in.

Infrastructure > Devboxes lets root administrators enable or disable command,
build, preview, and tunnel workloads per runner. New runners default to those
four workload types enabled. Disabling a type stops new matching jobs from being
claimed on that runner; it does not interrupt a running job or act as a
security permission for root workspace members who can submit generic commands.
The dashboard keeps switches unavailable until the
`20260928130000_devbox_runner_features.sql` migration is applied. Its Update CLI
action queues an update for an online runner, then the agent restarts as above.
The Restart agent action and `ttr box restart` queue a typed maintenance job
that exits the agent after successful acknowledgement; the installed service
manager starts it again. These actions restart the agent process, not the
operating system.
Judge defaults off. Enabling it requires a recent heartbeat reporting a
verified sandbox runtime and at least one pinned, cached language image.
Existing Devbox host commands remain separate from Judge submissions.

The same dashboard stores a runner's Judge capacity budget. Defaults reserve
at most 50% of host CPU and 25% of host memory, with one sandbox and one
instance at a time. Each sandbox defaults to 1 GB, 30 seconds, and 64
processes. Administrators can adjust these limits per machine. These settings
are enforced on each Judge container by Docker cgroups, with a conservative
free-memory check before each case. The platform claim function caps concurrent
Judge runs on a runner at the lower of its sandbox and instance maxima. Each
container receives a share of the host CPU and memory budget divided by that
ceiling. A managed agent can dispatch independent Judge jobs concurrently within
the configured process-wide sandbox budget. These settings do
not limit the current trusted host commands, builds, previews, or tunnels.

### Stale run reaper

Runs left `running` or `cancel_requested` after an agent crash, watchdog exit,
SIGKILL, or a claim response the agent never received would otherwise count
against that capacity forever. `private.reap_stale_devbox_runs` finishes them:

- `cancel_requested` unacknowledged for 10 minutes becomes `cancelled`;
- a run past `started_at + timeout_seconds + 5 minutes` becomes `failed`;
- a run started over 10 minutes ago on a missing or revoked runner, or one
  without a heartbeat for 10 minutes, becomes `failed`.

Reaped runs release an unused non-kept lease and record a `reaped` run event with
the reason. Every claim reaps up to 25 of the claiming runner's stale runs
before counting capacity, so both the Cloudflare control Worker and the web
poll route free slots without a scheduler. Runs without a timeout on a healthy
runner (long `serve` or `tunnel` jobs) are never reaped. Disabling a runner's
heartbeat takes it offline, so its active runs are reaped after 10 minutes.

**MANUAL sweep or on-claim self-reap only.** No trigger schedules a global
sweep today. Runners that never claim again retain their stale runs until an
authorized operator invokes `GET` or `POST /api/cron/devboxes/reap-stale-runs`
with `Authorization: Bearer $CRON_SECRET`. Each call reaps at most 200 runs
across all runners and returns `{ limit, reaped }`.

Adding a Cloudflare Cron Control trigger is a follow-up under the billable-work
rules: bounded calls/retries, idempotent progress, terminal scheduling and a
tested durable stop fence. Do not add a Vercel cron or pg_cron entry. Regression
coverage lives in `apps/database/supabase/tests/devbox-stale-run-reaper.sql`
and the route test.

## Judge setup

The Judge executor requires a Docker engine with the `runsc` gVisor runtime
registered, working CPU/memory/process cgroup limits, and locally cached OCI
images pinned to SHA-256 digests. The CLI fails readiness when these are absent
or the Docker engine is rootless with resource enforcement not verified. gVisor
currently requires a Linux host or Linux VM. Do not enable Judge on a machine
that has only the default Docker runtime.

Configure the languages you want with a JSON map of language names to pinned
image references. Supported adapters are Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C,
C++, Java, Rust, Go, Ruby, and PHP. The chosen image must contain that
language's runtime or compiler plus a POSIX shell and `base64` for compiled
languages. Pull each digest on the host before connecting. Then run:

```bash
export TUTURUUU_JUDGE_IMAGES='{"python":"python@sha256:<digest>","cpp":"gcc@sha256:<digest>"}'
ttr box judge doctor --images "$TUTURUUU_JUDGE_IMAGES"
ttr box connect --service --judge-images "$TUTURUUU_JUDGE_IMAGES"
```

Replace the placeholder digests with full verified 64-character values. The
connect command saves the map with the runner token in the restricted local
environment file used by the service. Its dashboard link opens the exact
runner row in Infrastructure. After the heartbeat reports Judge readiness,
review the host budget and enable Judge. Workspaces consume the platform Judge
capacity through Learn; they do not register or control the physical runner.

The executor runs one case at a time without network access or host mounts,
with a read-only image, dropped capabilities, no new privileges, a non-root
user, bounded temporary storage, and per-case CPU, memory, process, time, and
output limits. Compiled languages compile inside the same sandbox. Source and
hidden cases are stored in the private platform schema; learner results expose
only the aggregate pass count and visible case outcomes. A failed or missing
sandbox readiness check leaves Judge unavailable.

### Recover a Lima Judge VM after disk errors

On macOS, a full host disk can leave a Lima guest's ext4 root filesystem
read-only. If writes fail with `Read-only file system` or the VM stops before
SSH is ready, restore host free space first. Keep the VM disk and runner token
files. Check `df -h` on the host and remove only known rebuildable caches or
clean, merged worktrees.

If the guest remains read-only, stop the VM before checking its disk. On an
APFS host, make a copy-on-write backup, then attach the raw disk without
mounting it:

```bash
judge_instance=ttr-judge
limactl stop --force "$judge_instance"
judge_disk="$HOME/.lima/$judge_instance/disk"
cp -c "$judge_disk" "$judge_disk.pre-fsck"
diskutil image attach --noMount "$judge_disk"
```

Find the ext4 root partition in the `diskutil` output (for example,
`/dev/disk4s1`). Install the bottled `e2fsprogs` package if needed. Run the
read-only check first, then repair **that partition** with the block device
path, not the raw `/dev/rdisk*` path:

```bash
brew install --force-bottle e2fsprogs
e2fsck_bin="$(brew --prefix e2fsprogs)/sbin/e2fsck"
"$e2fsck_bin" -n /dev/disk4s1
"$e2fsck_bin" -y /dev/disk4s1
"$e2fsck_bin" -fn /dev/disk4s1
diskutil eject /dev/disk4
limactl start "$judge_instance"
```

Replace the example disk identifiers with those from your attach output. The
final check must report a clean filesystem. Verify guest writes and the runner
service before deleting the backup. If the host fills again, repair the host
space problem before restarting the VM; repeated restarts can corrupt more
guest data. See [Lima's offline fsck guidance](https://github.com/lima-vm/lima/discussions/2104)
for the underlying disk-image procedure.

Remove a runner from the cluster from the runner host with its runner token:

```bash
TUTURUUU_DEVBOX_RUNNER_TOKEN=<runner-token> ttr box shutdown
```

Shutdown deletes the runner's server-side token rows and marks the runner
revoked. If the host installed a systemd or launchd runner service, stop and
disable that service as well so the OS does not keep restarting an invalid
agent process.

Run heavy commands remotely:

```bash
ttr box run -- bun validate
ttr box run -- bun sb:reset
ttr box run -- bun test:e2e
ttr box build --cwd apps/web
```

By default, `ttr box run` creates an auto lease, waits for an authenticated
runner to claim the job, streams recorded logs after completion, and releases
the lease after one-off work. Use `--keep` for repeated sync/run work:

```bash
ttr box run --keep --preview-port 7803 -- bun test:e2e
ttr box sync --lease <lease-id> --watch
ttr box preview --lease <lease-id> --port 7803
ttr box release <lease-id>
```

## Build, Serve, And Tunnel

Use `ttr box build` for common build workloads without spelling the full remote
command every time:

```bash
ttr box build
ttr box build --cwd apps/web
ttr box build --build-command "bun turbo:local run build -F @tuturuuu/web"
```

Use `ttr box serve` when the remote devbox should build an app, start the
server, and keep the run alive. It defaults to `apps/web` on port `7803`, stores
the preview port on the run, and returns immediately unless `--wait` is passed:

```bash
ttr box serve --cwd apps/web --port 7803
ttr box preview --lease <lease-id> --port 7803
ttr box logs <run-id>
ttr box stop <run-id>
```

`ttr box stop`, `ttr box logs`, and lease release act only on runs and leases
created by the signed-in user; another member's ids return 404. Stopping a queued
run cancels it immediately, a running run moves to `cancel_requested` for its
agent, and finished runs are never changed. Repeating an owner stop on a
`cancel_requested` or `cancelled` run returns its current cancellation without
rewriting timestamps; retries cannot postpone stale-run reaping. Foreign ids
still return 404, including cancelled or finished runs. Owner stops that race
completion return the observed final status without a write. Infrastructure
administrators use the same stable retry and final-status behavior and can
stop any active run from the dashboard. Regression coverage lives in
`apps/web/src/lib/devboxes/store-scoping.test.ts`.

`ttr box build`, `ttr box serve`, and `ttr box tunnel` do not set a remote
command timeout by default. Pass `--timeout <duration>` only when the run should
be killed automatically.

To expose a served app through a Cloudflare tunnel, keep the token in a local
environment variable and pass the variable name to the devbox. The queued
command references `$CLOUDFLARED_TOKEN`; the raw token is delivered only as
run-scoped env and is redacted from logs.

```bash
export CLOUDFLARED_TOKEN=<token-from-cloudflare>
ttr box serve --cloudflared --cloudflared-token-env CLOUDFLARED_TOKEN
ttr box tunnel --cloudflared-token-env CLOUDFLARED_TOKEN
```

`ttr box tunnel` runs a dockerized `cloudflare/cloudflared` container with host
networking on the runner. The command policy blocks inline `cloudflared
--token ...` arguments, so operators should use `--cloudflared-token-env` or
another local environment variable indirection rather than pasting raw tokens
into commands.

## Container Boundary

The current agent starts brokered commands directly on the host. The command
policy blocks several destructive command forms, but is not a sandbox. These
machines must be operated as trusted infrastructure. Docker-backed commands
create their own containers only when the requested command does so.

Allowed remote workflows include:

- `bun validate`, `bun test`, and package-local Bun commands
- `bun test:e2e` and Docker-backed Playwright workflows
- `bun sb:start`, `bun sb:reset`, `bun sb:up`, and `bun sb:typegen`

Blocked defaults include privileged Docker containers, Docker prune-all style
commands, absolute host mounts, `sudo`, and host-destructive filesystem
operations.

## Env And Secrets

Remote env is explicit. Local `.env*` files are never synced automatically.
The setup command only prepares ignored app env files inside the runner
checkout so local Supabase-backed apps and E2E workflows can use that runner's
own Supabase stack.

```bash
ttr box run --env DATABASE_URL=postgres://remote -- bun validate
ttr box run --database-url-env DEVBOX_DATABASE_URL -- bun validate
ttr box serve --database-url-env DEVBOX_DATABASE_URL
ttr box run --env-file .env.remote -- bun test:e2e
ttr box env set --lease <lease-id> API_TOKEN=value
ttr box env unset --lease <lease-id> API_TOKEN
```

Brokered env values are scoped to the run or lease, delivered only to the
claimed runner, and redacted from command logs.

For split-resource development, run Supabase or another database on one devbox,
publish its reachable URL as `DEVBOX_DATABASE_URL` on the operator machine, and
queue the app devbox with `--database-url-env DEVBOX_DATABASE_URL`. This lets a
database-heavy runner and a Next.js runner share work while the current machine
only brokers commands and opens previews.

## Runner scheduling and hosted environments

Agents keep heartbeats on a 20-second cadence while dispatching independent jobs
concurrently, with at most eight active jobs. Judge cases share a process-wide
sandbox budget and always use fresh isolated containers. Each case reserves
`1 / parallelLimit` of the host budget, so mixed jobs cannot each claim the
whole memory or CPU allocation. Eligible smaller reservations can pass a waiting
full-budget case. Infrastructure failures cancel queued cases and wait for
already admitted commands and container cleanup before reporting failure.
Regression coverage lives in `devbox-sandbox-slots.test.ts` and
`devbox-judge-case-batch.test.ts`. Maintenance and CLI
restart jobs drain active work before changing the agent. An execution failure
stops new dispatch and drains already active work before the agent exits. Heartbeats
continue during that drain, and local completions wake idle claim polling. The
parent scheduling client omits Playground capabilities until both heartbeat
contracts support them; `devbox-agent-capabilities.test.ts` exercises its emitted
body against both current handlers. Both heartbeat handlers (`apps/web` and the
`devbox-control` Worker) also accept an optional `executionMode`
(`trusted` or `judge-only`), an optional `protocols.commitRun` list of envelope
versions (integers 1-100), and an optional `isolation` summary: `checkedAt` plus
the boolean checks `dedicatedUser`, `privateTokenDirectory`, `protectedService`,
`dedicatedDockerSocket`, `gvisorDefault` and `noGeneralDockerGroup`. Unknown keys
and wrong types are still rejected. These fields are self-reported and advisory:
they are stored for operators and later claim matching, never used to grant
features or authorize a runner. Agents send them only after both handlers are
deployed. Judge readiness probes are cached for ten minutes and refreshed in the background; execution still fails
closed if required isolation or language images are unavailable.

Agent HTTP calls are bounded. Heartbeat, claim, event, completion and shutdown
requests time out after 15 seconds (playground file sync after 30 seconds), and
the timeout also covers reading the response body. Network errors, timeouts,
`408`, `425`, `429` and `5xx` responses are transient: heartbeats retry with
jittered exponential backoff (never slower than the 20-second heartbeat
interval), and claims back off up to 60 seconds without crashing. Event and
completion uploads retry up to three times. A replayed completion that finds the
run already finished (`404` on a retry) counts as delivered. Rejected tokens and
other `4xx` responses still stop the agent for operator action. If no heartbeat
succeeds for six intervals (two minutes), the agent drains active jobs and exits
non-zero. A separate timer exits the process with code `75` after twice that
window if an await stays wedged, so the service manager's `Restart=always`
recovers the agent instead of leaving it hung with a stale heartbeat. Regression
coverage, including a real socket that never answers, lives in
`devbox-agent-network.test.ts`.

Trusted jobs run as the leader of their own process group. A timeout
(`--timeout`) or a remote stop (`ttr box stop <run-id>`) sends `SIGTERM` to the
whole group: shells, Docker CLIs and test workers, not only the direct child.
Anything still running after a 10-second grace period gets `SIGKILL`. The
claiming agent observes a stop through the events endpoint, which returns
`cancelRequested` to the runner that owns the run, about every 10 seconds per
job. A stopped run completes as `cancelled` with exit `143`; a timeout completes
as `failed` with exit `124`. On `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` the agent claims nothing
new, finishes its active jobs while heartbeating, and exits `0`. A second signal
also stops active trusted jobs through their process groups. Generated systemd
units use `KillMode=mixed` (only the agent receives the stop signal) and
`TimeoutStopSec=600`; launchd plists use `ExitTimeOut` 600. Re-render existing
units with `ttr box repair` to pick these up. Regression coverage lives in
`devbox-job-process.test.ts` and `devbox-agent-stop.test.ts`. Signals only ever
target the job's process group. Once the group is gone the agent does not signal
the bare PID, because the operating system may have reused it for an unrelated
process.

Judge sandboxes carry a `dev.tuturuuu.devbox.judge=1` label and an owner label
derived from a hash of the runner token. Docker keeps a container running after
the agent dies (watchdog exit, `SIGKILL`, crash). So when an agent with
`TUTURUUU_JUDGE_IMAGES` configured starts, it removes up to 100 of its own
runner's labelled containers before claiming work. Dedicated playground pool
processes skip this step, and other runners on the same host keep their
containers. Regression coverage lives in `devbox-judge-containers.test.ts`.

Platform-managed playground workers opt in through operator configuration. They
require gVisor and pinned language image digests, run unprivileged without host
credentials, and disable network access by default. Project environments retain
dependencies while warm. A configured `TUTURUUU_PLAYGROUND_POOL_ID` dedicates the
agent process to Playground: Judge readiness is false and Judge execution fails
before Docker admission, so warm environments cannot double the Judge host budget.
Idle/max-age eviction waits for an active project run and holds the pool lock;
near-expiry containers are replaced before admitting another bounded run. Failed
starts remove their exact owned name, retaining quarantined capacity when Docker
cannot confirm removal. Environments expire after fifteen idle minutes and have a two-hour
maximum lifetime. Environment count is bounded by the runner's resource limits.
A failed container removal retains its capacity reservation until a successful
removal or healthy Docker inventory confirms the container is absent. Failed
startup orphan cleanup blocks new environments and is retried on the next
admission. Creation and stop removal share the same pool lock. Same-project runs
serialize synchronization, execution and saves; stop invalidates queued runs
without waiting for a running command. Stopping waits for admitted creation, with a fifteen-second
wait bound; a timeout reports an unconfirmed stop and retains capacity ownership.
It does not wait for the arbitrary project command to finish. Python helpers use
the pinned image PATH, including images that install Python under `/usr/local/bin`.
A failed background save emits a fixed diagnostic and makes the run report
incomplete persistence rather than silently claiming success. These lifecycle
rules are covered by `devbox-playground-sandbox.test.ts`.
File inventories and changed bytes are exported separately; credentials and
runner metadata never enter project files. File/directory conflicts are checked
against every path ancestor, and preview paths reject traversal before URL
normalization. Export transport permits the worst-case JSON escaping of a valid
two-MiB text project; unsupported paths or oversized files report the offending
file instead of failing with an opaque schema error. The schema and Python
export contracts cover these rules. The platform must provide its signed
file-save callback before enabling the hosted playground workload. The scheduling
primitives alone reject the reserved hosted Playground envelope without running a
host command; its HTTP adapter ships together with the canonical file-save API.
The typed-adapter regression in `devbox-runner-judge.test.ts` verifies hosted execution uses the sandbox and canonical authenticated callback, while malformed envelopes never fall through to host execution.

Use focused SDK agent, Judge and sandbox-slot tests for scheduling changes. A
passing mock test does not establish real sandbox startup latency; measure cold
and warm execution on a configured gVisor runner before advertising timings.
Do not fall back to ordinary Docker isolation when gVisor is missing.

## Resource queue offload cancellation

`ttr resources run --offload auto -- <command>` may queue locally only before
remote creation starts, or after a definite server rejection. A lost response,
malformed success acknowledgement, or unexpected error after creation starts
exits nonzero and never repeats the command locally. When the acknowledgement
contains a run ID, the CLI requests cancellation of that same run.

Each offload sends a fresh client operation ID as `idempotencyKey`. The create
handler dedupes on (actor, key), so a retried create returns the original run;
reusing a key for a different command returns 409. When creation is interrupted,
times out or fails without a definite rejection, the CLI calls
`POST /api/v1/devboxes/runs/stop-by-key`, which is scoped to the caller's runs.
A 404 can mean the create is still in flight, so the CLI retries up to three
times within a 10-second budget. If cancellation is still unconfirmed, it prints
the operation key; find the run with `ttr box list` and stop it with
`ttr box stop <run-id>`. A stop request alone does not prove the remote process
has exited.

Keyed creates are accepted only once key storage is confirmed:
`private.devbox_run_idempotency_ready()` reports the unique (actor, key) index as
valid, and the schema cache knows the column. Until then, the handler returns
503 with `code: DEVBOX_IDEMPOTENCY_UNAVAILABLE` before writing anything. The CLI
treats that coded 503 as a definite rejection, so `--offload auto` queues
locally. Any other 503 stays ambiguous. Unkeyed creates never consult key
storage.

The proxy exempts trusted CLI identities from its general rate limit, so keyed
creates and `runs/stop-by-key` each have a per-actor limit of 30 requests per
minute (`apps/web/src/lib/devboxes/rate-limits.ts`). A 429 is a definite
rejection.

SIGINT and SIGTERM remain terminal through every creation outcome, including a
later rejection, and return 130 and 143 respectively. Cancellation or the overall
deadline is checked before each log page and status request. Fleet, creation,
status, log and stop requests each have a 15-second bound; follow requests also
respect the remaining overall deadline. Repeated control-plane failures request
a remote stop and exit nonzero. A stalled stop request cannot hold the CLI open
indefinitely.

The focused `resources-offload-interruption.test.ts` suite covers rejected and
malformed creation after interruption, ambiguous acknowledgements, stalled log
pages, cancellation between full pages, and SDK transport abort signals.
`resources-offload-operation-key.test.ts` covers an accepted create whose
acknowledgement is lost after Ctrl-C, an in-flight create, and the unconfirmed
notice. `store-run-idempotency.test.ts` covers server-side dedupe and key races.
These fixtures do not establish hosted runner acceptance.

### Run log cursor

Run events carry a dense per-run `seq`. A `BEFORE INSERT` trigger allocates it
by updating, or creating, the run's `devbox_run_event_cursors` row. That row
lock is held until the writer commits, so commit order equals sequence order for
every writer (web, infrastructure and SQL functions). The logs route pages
`seq > offset` and returns the last `seq` as `next`. Because sequences start at 1,
older clients that send raw-row offsets keep working. Paging by a `created_at`
offset could repeat one line and skip another that committed late with an
earlier timestamp.

Events written before the migration keep positions `1..n` in the
`(created_at, id)` order readers already used, and later events start at `n + 1`.
The cursor row records `legacy_rows` and `legacy_numbered`. The route keeps the
legacy `created_at` paging for a run until the two match (and when the cursor
table is missing), then switches to `seq` with consistent offsets.

#### Rollout without a long table lock

The migrations are split so the run events table is never exclusively locked for
longer than a catalog change:

| Migration | Step | Lock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `20261024030000` | nullable `seq`, cursor table, triggers, functions, `NOT VALID` constraints | brief `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, `lock_timeout` 5 s |
| `030100`, `030150`, `030200` | unique `(run_id, seq)`, partial unsequenced and unique `(actor_id, idempotency_key)` indexes | `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, one statement per file |
| `030300` | backfill of at most 50 000 events in 5 000-row calls | row locks; same-run appends wait |
| `030350` | `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` once no event is unsequenced | `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` |

The migration runner wraps a multi-statement file in one transaction, and
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside one. Each concurrent index is
therefore the only statement in its file. If a concurrent build fails, drop the
invalid index before re-running, because `if not exists` would skip it.

Check production size before applying (read-only):

```sql
select count(*) as events,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('private.devbox_run_events')) as total_size,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('private.devbox_run_events')) as heap_size,
  (select count(distinct run_id) from private.devbox_run_events) as runs
from private.devbox_run_events;
```

If more than 50 000 events exist, `030300` leaves the rest for this one-time job.
Run it with the service role or as the database owner, one call per transaction,
until it returns 0, and then validate:

```sql
select private.backfill_devbox_run_event_seq(5000);  -- repeat until 0
alter table private.devbox_run_events
  validate constraint devbox_run_events_seq_present;
```

Each call numbers at most 5 000 events and locks only the cursor row of the run
it is numbering.

`store-run-logs.test.ts` models a late commit and the legacy-to-sequence switch.
`apps/database/supabase/tests/devbox-run-log-cursor.sql` checks density, forged
sequences, validation, readiness and key constraints. To reproduce the
concurrency boundary itself, use two sessions on a private socket-only Postgres
cluster (`initdb`, then `pg_ctl -o "-c listen_addresses='' -k <dir>"`):

1. Session A runs `begin`, inserts an event for a run and sleeps before `commit`.
2. Session B inserts an event for the same run.
3. A reader pages `seq > cursor` before and after both commit.

Before the migration the `created_at` reader sees `B,B`. After it, B blocks
until A commits, and the reader sees `A,B`.

## Cache Policy

Runners use named cache volumes for Bun installs, Turbo, Playwright browsers,
Supabase Docker state, package manager cache, and optional `node_modules`.
Cache keys include the repo fingerprint, lockfile hash, runtime image digest,
platform, command profile, Bun/Node versions, and cache schema version.

Cleanup runs on runner startup, after runs, and during heartbeat maintenance.
The runner evicts incompatible caches first, including legacy Bun install caches
when the Bun version, lockfile hash, package profile, or cache schema changes.
It then enforces cache budgets with least-recently-used eviction while keeping a
small set of recent compatible caches to avoid thrashing.

Operators can inspect and prune cache metadata:

```bash
ttr box cache list
ttr box cache doctor
ttr box cache prune
```

## Access

Remote devbox API routes require a Tuturuuu CLI/app session and root workspace
membership with `workspace_members.type = 'MEMBER'`. Guests and non-root
workspace users cannot create runs, leases, previews, or runner tokens.

## Local Executable Verification

For local source CLI development, use an isolated CLI config and disposable resource home so production CLI and scheduler state stay separate. `bun ttr` invokes the trusted global CLI; it does not run source. Use the explicit source entry below:

```bash
bun sb:status
docker exec supabase_db_tuturuuu psql -U postgres -d postgres -tAc "select to_regclass('private.devbox_leases'), exists (select 1 from supabase_migrations.schema_migrations where version = '20260603171600')"
TUTURUUU_CONFIG=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-config.json TTR_RESOURCES_HOME=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-resources bun packages/sdk/src/cli/index.ts login --base-url http://localhost:7803
TUTURUUU_CONFIG=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-config.json TTR_RESOURCES_HOME=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-resources bun packages/sdk/src/cli/index.ts box agent register --name local-devbox
TUTURUUU_CONFIG=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-config.json TTR_RESOURCES_HOME=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-resources bun packages/sdk/src/cli/index.ts box agent start --token <runner-token>
TUTURUUU_CONFIG=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-config.json TTR_RESOURCES_HOME=/tmp/ttr-devbox-local-resources bun packages/sdk/src/cli/index.ts box run -- bun --version
```

The final command should print the remote command logs and exit with the remote
command's exit code. In local Supabase, `private.devbox_runs.status` should end
as `succeeded` with `exit_code = 0`.

## Production Readiness

The production API needs migration
`20260603171600_create_private_devboxes.sql` before any `ttr box` command can
create leases or runs. If the CLI prints a schema-cache error such as
`private.devbox_leases` not being found, first confirm the production migration
workflow ran for the deployed SHA. If the table exists but PostgREST still
returns the schema-cache error, refresh the schema cache from Supabase SQL
Editor:

```sql
select to_regclass('private.devbox_leases');
select version from supabase_migrations.schema_migrations
where version = '20260603171600';
notify pgrst, 'reload schema';
```

Fleet selection rejects combining `--all` with explicit runner IDs. Maintenance
is deferred when a runner does not report its hostname. Fleet upgrades honor
`--timeout`; a timed-out run requests cancellation and reports whether that
request succeeded. Verify its run and lease before retrying or touching another
runner, since a stop request does not prove immediate process termination.


## Runtime Acceptance Diagnostics

Judge capacity discovery runs a strict four-second `docker info` metadata probe
before allocating a sandbox. A failure reports a fixed timeout, spawn
(not found, permission denied, or other), numeric exit, signal, or missing-exit
classification. These diagnostics omit Docker hosts, command arguments, raw
output, and provider error messages. A timeout is not proof that the engine is
absent: inspect the owning CI job and runner lifecycle before repairing or
retrying. Successful discovery still requires registered gVisor, enforced
cgroups, and reported CPU/memory capacity. Mocked process tests verify the
classification and failure boundary; they do not verify a runner's Docker engine.

The Lettin persistence browser regression separately reports project-navigation
confirmation and the notebook-button action, retaining their existing deadlines
and assertions. Phase failures emit an allowlisted error name and a fixed message
summary rather than authenticated URLs or response bodies. A runner shutdown
without a final assertion report leaves the underlying cause unproven. Preserve
allocated fixtures until successful final cleanup or independently verified
resource absence, and use the next exact-source CI result for runtime evidence.

### Composing devbox claim migrations

Apply trust pools (`20261023100000`), drain hardening (`20261023103000`),
mode admission (`20261024094600`), then stale-run reaping (`20261024095000`).
The final claim keeps the mode and drain admission predicates and lease move,
and reaps at most 25 runs for the claiming runner after acquiring its advisory
lock and before counting capacity. Run the trust-pool, drain-hardening, mode
admission and stale-run reaper pgTAP suites against this combined sequence;
validating each migration in isolation cannot prove the final claim behavior.

Reaping releases a non-kept lease only after every queued, running or
cancel-requested sibling finishes. Multiple runs may reuse one lease; a stale
run cannot invalidate a healthy sibling's next claim. The reaper locks affected
leases in ID order before checking siblings in a fresh statement snapshot;
enqueue locks the lease for sharing and rejects inactive leases after waiting. The stale-run reaper
pgTAP suite covers queued and running siblings and final-sibling release.

For the lease race regression, run
`supabase/fixtures/devbox-reaper-lease-race.sql` as `supabase_admin` inside the
repository isolated local database before its lifecycle cleanup. It opens two
committed sessions to prove each lease-lock winner. Normal Supabase pgTAP uses
the restricted `postgres` role, which cannot use dblink with loopback trust
authentication. Keep this privileged fixture inside a disposable local stack;
its setup commits rows and its teardown removes only its actor's devbox rows.
The lifecycle's full database cleanup removes the test account and its automatic
workspace membership.

## Trusted command execution boundary

General devbox jobs intentionally execute caller-selected binaries and argv on
trusted infrastructure. Only verified CLI app sessions or authenticated Supabase
sessions with `MEMBER` membership in the root workspace can submit them through
`/api/v1/devboxes/runs`. Membership in another workspace, root guest membership,
and pull-request content alone do not authorize submission. Root members are
trusted to execute code on enabled fleet runners; command-policy deny rules are
operational guardrails, not a sandbox or an executable allowlist.

The API persists the verified actor with the command in `private.devbox_runs`.
Private tables have RLS enabled, and the claim RPC is restricted to `service_role`.
Both the Web polling endpoint and the control Worker authenticate a hashed,
non-revoked runner token and recheck its owner's root membership. The Worker
supports heartbeat, poll, connect and internal wake notifications, not arbitrary
job submission. Runner feature selection, active leases and trust-pool constraints
limit claims. Host-side execution fences reject Judge and playground envelopes
on ordinary trusted runners, and generic commands on Judge-only runners.
Learner source reaches the dedicated Judge/playground paths, not generic host
execution. Keep those pools and their credentials separate.

The exact-commit envelope validates a full SHA and clean relative directory,
fetches origin branches and requires the SHA to be reachable from an origin
branch before making a private detached worktree. This proves provenance, not
that project code or a branch is safe: root members must review what they submit.
An explicit interpreter such as `sh -c` remains supported for these trusted users.

The process launcher always uses `shell: false` and a separate argv array.
It rejects control characters and shell metacharacters in the executable and NUL
in arguments. Shell syntax in ordinary arguments remains literal; these checks
do not restrict what an explicitly selected interpreter can execute. Regression
coverage is in `packages/sdk/src/cli/devbox-job-process.test.ts`,
`devbox-runner-trust.test.ts`, and `devbox-commit-run.test.ts`; API authorization
coverage is in the devbox runs route tests. CodeQL command-line-injection alerts
at this launcher require review of the authenticated execution boundary rather
than treating `shell: false` alone as proof of safety. Source review does not
verify deployed grants, runner configuration, or token custody.
